10.1002_eem2.70447: Cobalt‐based Prussian blue analogs (CoHCC) have emerged as highly promising anode materials for potassium‐ion batteries due to their open framework structure, suitable potassium‐ion insertion potential, and high theoretical capacity. However, the intrinsically low electronic conductivity of CoHCC, its tendency for particle agglomeration during traditional synthesis, and the uncontrollable particle size have severely restricted its potassium‐ion storage performance. This study reports a hydroxylated MXene‐assisted in situ synthesis strategy for constructing ultrafine CoHCC nanoparticles anchored on a Ti 3 C 2 T x MXene substrate (CoHCC@MX) as a high‐performance potassium‐ion battery anode. The –OH groups on the MXene surface serve as effective anchoring sites, enabling uniform nucleation and growth of CoHCC nanocrystals while preventing particle aggregation. The MXene substrate forms a continuous metallic conductive network, significantly enhancing electron transport and alleviating the poor conductivity of pristine CoHCC. Density functional theory calculations indicate strong interfacial electronic coupling between the –OH‐functionalized MXene and CoHCC, which not only stabilizes the composite structure but also inhibits the dissolution of active materials. The optimized CoHCC@MX‐1.0 composite anode delivers a high reversible capacity of 289.3 mAh g −1 after 1000 cycles at 500 mA g −1 , and exhibits excellent rate performance. When paired with a K 1.92 Fe[Fe(CN) 6 ] 0.94 ·0.5H 2 O cathode to assemble a full cell, it achieves a high energy density of 228.1 Wh kg −1 and retains 80.8% of its energy after 600 cycles. This work underlines the crucial role of functionalized MXene in interface engineering, providing a promising design strategy for advanced potassium‐ion storage materials.
10.1021_acsapm.6c01845: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide The increasing occurrence of endocrine-disrupting compounds (EDCs) in aquatic environments demands efficient removal strategies. This study evaluated organic and hybrid molecularly imprinted (MIP) and nonimprinted polymers (NIP) as adsorbents for progesterone removal from aqueous media. Materials were characterized by thermogravimetric analysis, infrared spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. Adsorption studies revealed optimal performance at pH 4, with rapid equilibrium within 120 s, governed by pseudo-second-order kinetics and dual-site Langmuir–Freundlich behavior, indicating the coexistence of specific and nonspecific binding sites. The organic imprinted polymer (MIP-O) achieved the highest capacity (22.345 mg g –1 ), with a ∼15% advantage over nonimprinted counterparts, while hybrid materials (MIP-H and NIP-H) exhibited comparable performance, indicating reduced imprinting efficiency. Comprehensive thermodynamic analysis confirmed entropy-driven adsorption at elevated temperatures, while computational modeling revealed that binding is governed by cooperative hydrogen bonding between polymer carboxylic acid groups and progesterone carbonyls (Δ E = −18.5 kcal mol –1 ). The MIP-O also exhibited satisfactory reusability, retaining approximately 68% of its adsorption capacity after six adsorption–desorption cycles. These findings demonstrate that organic molecular imprinting provides superior selectivity and performance for steroidal contaminant removal, offering rational design principles for advanced water treatment adsorbents.
